Time tree: plants through time

Every lineage on the cited, dated tree, with the spores, pollen and gyrogonites placed where they first appear. Time runs upward, oldest at the bottom, drawn to true scale. Click a clade for its sources.

How the tree is built, and the key

Time runs upward, oldest at the bottom as in a rock column. Built from the R project's cited trees: every clade carries its status and sources (click a clade), and branch points sit at the clade's dated age (median over 20 random resolutions of the polytomies, dated with paleotree, minimum branch length 1 Myr). Lineages shows each lineage as a stem with the genera of each opened interval on it; Genera shows every whole-plant genus as a range bar on the dated synthesis tree, so alleged ancestors (grades, marked * or "grade") sit below the groups thought to descend from them. By default the bands are not to scale: opened intervals get equal height. Choose True scale to draw geologic time in proportion. Genus ranges and lineage origins are approximate and listed for hand-checking in the R project.

Spores and pollen

Drawn to relative size: a 40 µm spore is 10 px across, a 300 µm medullosan prepollen grain 72 px. Grains larger than 1 mm (the biggest megaspores) are drawn at 1/10 of their size inside a dashed ring. Gyrogonites are not to scale: at roughly half a millimetre or more, they keep their usual size here. Faint glyphs have no size on record yet and are drawn at a typical 44 µm.

Fossil diversity through time: spores, pollen and gyrogonites

Fossil record only. These charts count fossil dispersed genera from the rocks, not living plants; living species are in the separate panel. How many fossil genera of each kind this catalogue holds through the rock record, with spores split by parent group (bryophytes, lycophytes, ferns, megaspores apart) and pollen by gymnosperms against flowering plants. The default view is a set of accumulation curves: the running total of genera that have made their first appearance by each age, so each line only climbs, and its steep stretches are where many new genera enter. "Genera present" instead counts each genus from its first to its last appearance. Time runs left to right, oldest at the left. Hover for the counts; click to list the genera behind them. These are the genera gathered here, not every genus ever described, so the Pennsylvanian and Permian, where the catalogue is most complete, stand out partly for that reason.

Every spore genus: size through time

Across: size on a logarithmic scale, so each step of ten takes the same width and 15 µm miospores sit beside 3 mm megaspores. Up: geologic time, oldest at the bottom as in a rock column. Each box is one genus, from its smallest to largest size and from its first to last appearance. The shaded band is the interval this page shows; dots in it are measured species. In the spirit of Chaloner's (1967) histograms of spore size through time (Fig. 13.2 in Taylor, Taylor & Krings 2009). Click a box or dot to select it.

Chart after Chaloner (1967), who plotted spore diameters on a logarithmic scale through geologic time to show spores growing larger through the Devonian and splitting into micro- and megaspores: W. G. Chaloner, 1967, Spores and land-plant evolution, Review of Palaeobotany and Palynology 1: 83–93.

Milestones

Where more exists: survey reports, theses and other literature

A search (24 November 2026) of state geological surveys, the USGS, theses and dissertations, museum and slide collections, open datasets, and national surveys and journals abroad, in English, German, Dutch, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Polish, Czech, Russian, Ukrainian, Turkish, Chinese and other languages, for Pennsylvanian (late Carboniferous) spores and plants. Each entry says whether it could be read. Where it could, its spore and plant lists were extracted; those records appear in the genus cards above. Entries marked print only, catalogue entry only or site refused automated reading are the ones a person could help with: send a copy or a link below.

Help fill the gaps: send a document or photo

Much of what is known about Pennsylvanian spores and plants sits outside the journals: state geological survey bulletins and circulars, USGS open-file reports, theses and dissertations, field-trip guidebooks, coal-company and agency reports, museum catalogues, and slide collections. If you have, or know of, a document with spore counts, species lists, coal-ball or compression floras, localities or coal-bed correlations, please send it here. Documents in any language are welcome (German, French, Dutch, Spanish, Polish, Czech, Russian, Ukrainian, Turkish, Chinese and others); an original-language citation is fine. Each submission is read and checked before anything from it is added, and it is credited to its original authors. Send a citation and link if the document is online; upload a scan only if you have the right to share it.

Sign in to claude.ai with access to this page to send a document or photo. If you can only view the page, add a comment instead: a citation in a comment works just as well.

References behind this network

    How the dates were checked. Plant and organ genus names were checked against the Paleobiology Database. Spore genus names were checked against the type-species authorities in Balme's (1995) summary. In situ links take the year of the earliest study Balme cites for that record; spores were often seen in cones decades before the dispersed genus was named, so a link shows once both names exist. Organ-to-plant years are still approximate while their original papers are being traced.

    Cladograms and time tree are drawn from the R project SporaeDispersae: clade tables citing Kenrick & Crane (1997), Bateman et al. (1992), Crane (1985), Doyle & Donoghue (1986), Doyle (2006), Hilton & Bateman (2006), PPG I (2016), APG IV (2016) and the One Thousand Plant Transcriptomes Initiative (2019), each clade marked consensus, cited, polytomy, grade or affinity; dated in R with paleotree and ape. Clades marked "cited", the genus ranges and the calibrations are on the project's hand-check list.

    Habitat readings come from a synthesis of the literature (DiMichele & Phillips 1994; DiMichele et al. 1996; Looy et al. 2014 and others). The two Gondwanan habitats were added from background knowledge and are marked to verify.

    Cook a spore

    Sporopollenin is the toughest material plants make, but heat during burial slowly chars it. Set how hot the rock got and how long it stayed there.

    Yellowscore 3 / 7

    An illustration, not a calibrated model: peak heat matters most, and long time at modest heat adds a little. Palynologists read this darkening on a colour scale (the spore colour index) to judge how hot a rock has been.
